scenario: A 68-year-old man is bleeding after a bypass. He has been on a high dose of unfractionated heparin. The aPTT is very long. A classmate gives vitamin K because all anticoagulants reverse the same way.
question: What binds the heparin, and why is vitamin K the wrong reversal?
options: Vitamin K, because the aPTT is long
More heparin, to stabilize the clot
A fibrinolytic, to seal the bypass site
explanation:
Protamine binds heparin and reverses unfractionated heparin. It does not reverse warfarin. Heparin is a drug already in the blood. Protamine neutralizes it. Vitamin K lets the liver make factors and is the warfarin reversal, which takes time. Katzung BG, Vanderah TW. Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 15th ed. McGraw Hill; 2021.

Protamine binds the drug
Vitamin K, because the aPTT is long — A long aPTT from heparin is not a vitamin K problem.
Platelets, the heparin reversal product — Platelets do not bind heparin.
More heparin, to stabilize the clot — More heparin worsens bleeding.
A fibrinolytic, to seal the bypass site — A fibrinolytic would increase bleeding.
citation: Katzung BG, Vanderah TW. Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 15th ed. McGraw Hill; 2021.
